feedback: If a learner mixes the vocabulary (calls the bottom number the numerator), reconnect each number to its job on the shaded model before naming it.
If a learner reads the symbol as two separate numbers, read symbol to word to shaded amount as one quantity several times ('three-quarters').
activities.intendedInsight: Each part of the written symbol has a fixed job tied to the model, and the symbol, spoken words and diagram are three views of the same single quantity.
learnerActions: Look at 3/4 beside its shaded bar. Point to the numerator and say what it does ('the parts we took'); point to the denominator and say what it does ('the equal parts in one whole').
Point to the whole bar and explain it is the one whole that was cut up.
Answer the prompt 'What if the top number were bigger than the bottom?' and predict what the picture and the name would become.
Link the three forms both directions: write the symbol, say the words, shade the picture, and go back again.
activities.title: Label the fraction's jobs

feedback: Correct classification requires a reason: ask 'How do you know this is improper?' and expect 'the top is as big as or bigger than the bottom, so it is one whole or more.'

If matching or filling in is correct but the learner still cannot read 5/4 as one quantity greater than one, return to the builder and number line, because recognition and fluency practice alone does not by itself elicit construction of the single-number idea.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure classification and word-symbol matching show the vocabulary has attached to structure, not just to top/bottom positions.
learnerActions: Sort a set of fraction cards into unit, proper, improper and mixed, giving one example of each; remember a unit fraction (numerator 1, denominator more than 1, like 1/4) is a special kind of proper fraction, so place it in the unit tray and keep the proper tray for proper fractions whose numerator is greater than 1 (a card such as 1/1 equals one whole and goes in the improper tray).
Match spoken words to written symbols (for example 'three-quarters' to 3/4).
Fill in the missing number: a shaded picture shows ?/? parts; write both the numerator and the denominator.
Explain in your own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent.
activities.title: Classify and match for fluency
